title: De Fide Ad Gratianum Augustum Libri Quinque
author: Ambrose
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0022.stoa002.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.

passages.original: Assertio autem nostræ fidei haec esi, ut unum Deum esse dicamus : neque, at gentes, Filium separemus : neque ut Judxi, natum ex Patre ante tempora, et ex Virgine postea editum denegemus : neque ut a Sabellius, Patrem confundamus et Verbum; ut eumdem Patrem asseramus et Filium : neque ut Photinus, initium Filii ex Virgine disputemus : neque ut Arius, plures credendo et dissimiles potestates, plures deos gentili errore faciamus, quia scriptum esl : Audi, Israel, Dominus Deus tuus, Deus unus est (Deut. VI, 4).
passages.english: Now the assertion of our faith is this: that we say God is one; and that we do not, like the Gentiles, separate the Son; nor, like the Jews, deny that he was born of the Father before time and afterwards brought forth from the Virgin; nor, like Sabellius, confuse the Father and the Word, so as to assert that the Father and the Son are the same; nor, like Photinus, argue that the Son had his beginning from the Virgin; nor, like Arius, by believing in many and unlike powers, make many gods in the error of the Gentiles; for it is written: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God" (Deut. 6:4).
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "esi" = est, "at gentes" = ut gentes, "Judxi" = Judaei, "esl" = est; stray "a" before Sabellius omitted.

passages.original: 452 45. Eunomii personam defugiunt Ariani, sed ejns perfidiam asserunt, impietatem exsequuntur. Aiunt eum prodidisse effusius, quæ Arius scripserit. Magna cæcitatis effusio ! Auctorem probant, exsecutorem refutant. Itaque nunc in plures sese divisere formas. d Alii Eunomium , vel Aetium , alii Palladium , vel Demophilum atque Auxentium, vel perfidiæ hujus hæredes sequuntur, alii diversos.
passages.english: 45. The Arians shun the person of Eunomius, but they assert his faithlessness and carry out his impiety. They say that he set forth too lavishly what Arius had written. What a great outpouring of blindness! They approve the author and repudiate the one who carried [him] out. And so they have now split into many forms. Some follow Eunomius or Aetius, others Palladius, or Demophilus and Auxentius, or the heirs of this faithlessness; others [follow] various [leaders].
passages.notes: Leading "452" is a page number; stray "d" is a footnote mark.

passages.original: 48. Apostolus dicit imaginem Patris Christum esse; ait enim quod ipse sit imago Dei invisibilis, primogenitus universæ. creaturae (Coloss. I, 15). Primogenitus, inquit, non primocreatus; ut et genitus pro natura , et primus pro perpetuitate credatur. Alibi quoque Apostolus asseruit quod ipsum posuit hceredem omnium, per quem fecit et scecula, qui eat splendor gloriœ, et character substantiœ ejus (Hebr. I, 2 ). Imaginem Apostolus dicit, et Arius dicit esse dissimilem : cur imago, si similitudinem non habet? in piciuris homines nolunt esse dissimiles, et Arius dissimilem Patrem contendit Filio, et vult ut Pater dissimilem genuerit sui, quasi impotens qui generare similem non potuerit.
passages.english: 48. The Apostle says that Christ is the image of the Father; for he says that he is "the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation" (Col. 1:15). "Firstborn," he says, not "first-created"; so that he may be believed both "born" in respect of nature and "first" in respect of everlastingness. Elsewhere too the Apostle asserted that [God] "appointed him heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages, who is the radiance of his glory and the impress of his substance" (Heb. 1:2-3). The Apostle says "image," and Arius says [he] is unlike: why an image, if it has no likeness? In pictures people do not want [them] to be unlike, and Arius contends that the Father is unlike the Son, and would have the Father beget one unlike himself, as if powerless, as one who could not beget a like [son].

passages.original: 119. Sic nempe b nostri secundum Scripturas dixerunt Patres, qui etiam sacrilega dogmata ideo suis inserenda putaverc decretis, ut Arii perfidia ipsa se proderet; ne quasi fucis quibusdam et coloribus illita vetaretur. Fucum cnim faciunt, qui non audent explicare quod sentiunt. Censorie itaque impietas Ariana non expositione reseratur, sed damnatione detegitur;
passages.english: 119. Thus indeed our Fathers spoke according to the Scriptures, who also thought that the sacrilegious doctrines should be inserted into their decrees for this reason, that the faithlessness of Arius might betray itself and not be concealed, as though smeared with certain cosmetics and colours. For those make a false show who do not dare to set out what they think. And so the Arian impiety is not opened up by exposition but uncovered by condemnation, as by a censor's judgment;
passages.notes: "putaverc" read as putavere; "cnim" as enim. The Council of Nicaea is evidently meant.

passages.original: 123. Arius ergo dicit ; Erat quando non erat; sed Scriptura dicit, Erat, non dicit, non erat. DeuMque Joannes scripsit : In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum : hoc erat in principio apud Deum (Joan.
passages.english: 123. Arius, then, says: "There was when he was not"; but Scripture says "he was," it does not say "he was not." And John wrote: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God" (John
passages.notes: The citation runs on into the following passage (1:1-2).

passages.original: 125. Veniamus ad alia. Arius dicit: Antequam nascerelur, non erat: sed Scriptura dicit omnia esse per Filium. Quomodo ergo aliis dedit esse, qui non erat? Cum autem dicit impius, quando et ante, hæc utique dno verba tempus ostendunt.
passages.english: 125. Let us come to other points. Arius says: "Before he was born, he was not"; but Scripture says that all things exist through the Son. How then did he who did not exist give existence to others? And when the impious man says "when" and "before," these two words certainly indicate time.

passages.original: 128. Arius dicit : Ex alia substantia. Quæ igitur alia substantia æquatur Dei Filio, ut ex ipsa Dei Filius sit? Aut quomodo reprehendunt quia uos in Deo ant οὐσἱαν Græce, aut Latine substantiam dicimus, eum ex alia dicendo substantia a Dei esse Filium, etiam ipsi substantiam Dei esse confirment?
passages.english: 128. Arius says: "From another substance." What other substance, then, is equal to the Son of God, that the Son of God should be from it? Or how do they find fault because we speak of God's ousia in Greek or substantia in Latin, when, by saying that the Son of God is from another substance, they themselves confirm that God has a substance?

passages.original: 430. Arius dicit creaturam Dei Filium, non sicu cæleras creaturas. Quae enim creatura cnon sicut alia creatura non est ? Homo non ut Angelus, terra nou ut coelum, sol non ut aqua, lumen non ut tenebræ. Nihil ergo præferendo donavit, aed ad simplices decipiendos misero colore fraudem suæ ..pietatis obduxit.
passages.english: 130. Arius says the Son of God is a creature, but not as the other creatures. For what creature is not unlike another creature? Man is not as an angel, earth not as heaven, the sun not as water, light not as darkness. So by this qualification he granted nothing, but to deceive the simple he covered the fraud of his impiety with a wretched colouring.
passages.notes: "430" read as 130. The Latin "non sicut alia creatura non est" is awkward; rendered by sense.

passages.original: 131. Arius dicit mutabitem et convertibilem Dei Filium. Quomodo ergo PeS, si mutabilis; cum ipse dixerit: Ego sum, ego sum, et non sum mutatus (Malac. III, 6)?
passages.english: 131. Arius says the Son of God is mutable and changeable. How then is he God, if mutable, when he himself said: "I am, I am, and I have not changed" (Mal. 3:6)?

passages.original: lium fateri nolint, ut significavit Eusebius Nicomediensis, Recte igitur constitulum a Nicænis PP. verbumόμοοὑσιον, utpote hæresi oppositum et in Scriptura firmatum ; proindeque neglectis, quas isti fingunt de Sabellianis, retinendum.
passages.english: ...[that they are unwilling] to confess the Son, as Eusebius of Nicomedia indicated. Rightly, therefore, was the word *homoousios* [of the same substance] established by the Nicene Fathers, as being opposed to heresy and grounded in Scripture; and accordingly it is to be retained, disregarding the [objections] which these men invent concerning the Sabellians.
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-word ('lium', probably the end of 'Filium'); it appears to be an editorial summary or marginal heading rather than Ambrose's text. Scanning errors corrected: 'constitulum' read as 'constitutum', 'verbumόμοοὑσιον' as 'verbum ὁμοούσιον'. After 'quas' a noun (e.g. 'calumnias' or 'objectiones') seems implied or lost.

passages.original: 125. Nam quid est aliud, cur ὁμοούϭιον Patri nolint Filium dici, nisi quia nolunt verum Dei Filium confiteri ? sicut auctor ipsorum Eusebius Nicome- diensis b cpistola sua prodidit scribens: Si verum , inquit, Dei Filium et increatum dicimus, ὁμοούϭιον cum Patre incipimus confiteri. Hæc cum lecta esset epistola in concilio Nicuno, hoc verbum in tractatu Fidei posuerunt Patres, quia id viderunt adversariis esse formidini;
passages.english: 125. For what other reason is there why they are unwilling that the Son be called *homoousios* [of the same substance] with the Father, except that they are unwilling to confess [him] the true Son of God? As their own author, Eusebius of Nicomedia, disclosed in his letter, writing: "If," he says, "we call [him] the true and uncreated Son of God, we begin to confess [him] *homoousios* with the Father." When this letter had been read at the Council of Nicaea, the Fathers set this word in the statement of the Faith, because they saw that it was a source of dread to [their] adversaries;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'ὁμοούϭιον' read as 'ὁμοούσιον', 'Nicome- diensis' as 'Nicomediensis', 'cpistola' as 'epistola', 'Nicuno' as 'Nicæno'; the stray 'b' is a footnote mark. 'In tractatu Fidei' is rendered 'in the statement of the Faith', meaning the creed.

passages.original: 23 . Et bene scriptum est : Heri et hodie ipse est; ut Arii impietas astruendi sacrilegii locum invenire non posset. Qui cum tegeret in psalmo secundo dicentem Filio Patrem : Filius meus ea tu , ego hodie genui te (Psal. II, 7); annotavit hodie non heri, ad æternitatem divinæ generationis referens, quod de carnis assumptione memoratum est, sicut Paulus in Actibus apostolorum ait : Et nos vobis annuntiamus, quæ ad patres nostros repromissio facta est ; quOniaM hanc Deus adimplevit e filiis nostris , resuscitans Dominum Jesum Christum, sicut scriptum est in psalmo secundo : Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te (Act. XIII, 32 et Iseq.) Sancto igitur Spiritu repletus Apostolus, ut illam elideret sævitatem, ait: Neri et hodie ipse est, et in sœcula : Aeri, propter aeternitatem : hodie, propter corporis susceptionem.
passages.english: 23. And it is well written: "Yesterday and today he is the same," so that the impiety of Arius could find no room to build up its sacrilege. For when he read in the second psalm the Father saying to the Son, "You are my Son, today I have begotten you" (Ps. 2:7), he noted "today," not "yesterday," applying to the eternity of the divine generation what was said of the taking up of flesh, as Paul says in the Acts of the Apostles: "And we announce to you the promise that was made to our fathers, that God has fulfilled this for our children, raising up the Lord Jesus Christ, as it is written in the second psalm: You are my Son, today I have begotten you" (Acts 13:32-33). The Apostle therefore, filled with the Holy Spirit, to crush that savagery, says: "Yesterday and today he is the same, and for ever": "yesterday" because of eternity, "today" because of the taking on of the body.
passages.notes: "tegeret" read as legeret; "Neri"/"Aeri" = Heri. Citation is Heb. 13:8.

passages.original: 105. N.<m Filius Dei est contra d Hebionem, Viii... David est contra Manichæos : Filius Dei est contra Photinum, Filius David est contra Marcionem : Filius Dei ea contra Paulum Samosatenum : 570 Fillus David est eontra Valentinum : Filius Cet cst contra Arium atque Sabellium gentilis crroris h:<'redes: Dominus David fst contra Judtfos , qui Dei Filium in cante cerneates, hominem tantummodo impio rUe rore credebant.
passages.english: 105. That [he is] the Son of God is against Ebion; [that he is the Son of] David is against the Manichaeans. That [he is] the Son of God is against Photinus; that [he is] the Son of David is against Marcion. That [he is] the Son of God is against Paul of Samosata; that [he is] the Son of David is against Valentinus. That [he is] the Son of God is against Arius and Sabellius, heirs of pagan error. That [he is] the Lord of David is against the Jews, who, seeing the Son of God in the flesh, believed in their impious error that he was only a man.
passages.notes: The text is badly scanned. Readings adopted: 'Nam Filius Dei' (opening), 'Filius David' for 'Viii...', 'Filius Dei est' for 'Filius Cet cst', 'haeredes', 'Judaeos', 'in carne cernentes', 'errore'. The stray letters 'd' and 'h' are taken as footnote marks. '570' is a page number and has been omitted.

passages.original: Esto tamen, spiritu ausuque temerario metiri te velim ; unde, quæso, te metiar? Funiculum agrimensorium vidit propheta (EzecA. XL, 3), quo metiebatur angelus Jerusalem. Metiebatur tamen angelus, non Arius : metiebatur Jerusalem, non Deum. Et fortasse nec Jerusalem metiri poterat angelus; vir enim erat. Denique sic habes : Et allet)at'! OCulOs, et vidi : et ecce vir, et in manu ejus funiculus agrimensorius (Ibid.).
passages.english: Suppose, nevertheless, that I wished to measure you with a rash spirit and daring: with what, I ask, should I measure you? The prophet saw a surveyor's cord (Ezek. 40:3), with which an angel was measuring Jerusalem. Yet it was an angel who measured, not Arius; he measured Jerusalem, not God. And perhaps not even the angel could have measured Jerusalem, for he was a man. In short, this is what you have: 'And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, a man, and in his hand a surveyor's cord' (ibid.).
passages.notes: 'Et allet)at'! OCulOs' is read as 'Et elevavi oculos'. The opening, 'Esto tamen … velim', is somewhat elliptical.

passages.original: 233. b Viderint tamen quid faciant Ariani : ego te, Pater, si majorem omnibus dixero, injuriose te Luis operibus comparavi : si majorem Filio, ut Arius asserit, impie judicavi. De te prior erit ilia sententia, nam neque ulla fieri potest nisi ex comparatione prælatio, ncque præferri quisquam, nisi de quo prius fuerit judicatum.
passages.english: 233. Let the Arians, however, see to what they are doing. As for me, Father: if I call you greater than all things, I have insultingly compared you with your own works; if [I call you] greater than the Son, as Arius asserts, I have judged impiously. That verdict will be about you first, for there can be no preference except by comparison, nor can anyone be preferred except one about whom a judgement has first been made.
passages.notes: 'Luis' is read as 'tuis'. The stray 'b' is taken as a footnote mark. The sense of 'De te prior erit illa sententia' is uncertain: perhaps that any such verdict would itself pass judgement on the Father.

passages.original: 237. Paulus etiam de inferioribus dicit : Ex parte cognoscimus et ex parte eliam prophetamus (t Cor. XIII. 9). Arius dicit: Ex toto Deum, non ex parte cognovi. Inferior ergo Paulus, quam Arius; et vas electionis ex parte scit, vas perditionis totum scit : Scio, inquit, hominem, sive in corpore, 595 sive extra corpus nescio, Deus scit, quoniam raptus ext in paradisum, et audivit verba ineffabilia (II Cor.
passages.english: 237. Paul also says of lesser things: 'We know in part and we prophesy in part' (1 Cor. 13:9). Arius says: 'I have known God wholly, not in part.' So Paul is inferior to Arius: the vessel of election knows in part, the vessel of perdition knows the whole! [Paul] says: 'I know a man, whether in the body or outside the body I do not know, God knows, that he was caught up into paradise and heard unspeakable words' (2 Cor.
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-citation; the reference (12:4-5) continues in the following text. '595' is a page number and has been omitted.

passages.original: Sed non Arios raptus in caelum, quamvis 596 eum secutus sil, qui jactatione damnabili divina praesumeret, dicens : Ponam thronum meum super nubes, et ero simlis Altissimo (Esai. XIV, 14) ; sicut enim ille dixit: Ero similis Altissimo : sic et Arius altissimum Dei Filium sui similem vult videri' quem non in divinitatis æternæ majestate veneratur, sed ex carnis infirmitate mctitur.
passages.english: But Arius was not caught up into heaven, although he followed him who with damnable boasting presumed upon divine things, saying: 'I will set my throne above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High' (Isa. 14:14). For just as that one said, 'I will be like the Most High,' so Arius too wants the most high Son of God to seem like himself. He does not worship him in the majesty of eternal divinity, but measures him by the weakness of the flesh.
passages.notes: 'Arios' is read as 'Arius'. '596' is a page number and has been omitted.
